questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of tingling in hands and feet. She had a history of well-controlled HIV and pleural tuberculosis. She was taking tenofovir alafenamide, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir, and was in the second month of continuation phase with RIF/INH. She was adherent with both her HIV and TB medications. She also took oral contraceptives. Physical exam was unremarkable. Investigations: Hb 95 g/L, MCV 74.5fL AST 21 IU/L ALT 15 IU/L Normal electrolytes, bilirubin, and albumin Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin positive CD4 count 520/mm3 HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Drug adverse effect The clinical presentation of tingling in stocking glove distribution is consistent with INH-induced neurotoxicity. Her pregnancy could be the result of decreased levels of oral contraceptives due to pharmacologic interaction with rifampin. The vignette does not mention whether the patient is receiving pyridoxine, but pregnancy puts her at higher risk for pyridoxine deficiency.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q32

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman was prescribed clofazimine as part of her treatment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
questions.lead_in: What adverse effect of clofazimine should this patient be made aware of prior to initiating therapy?
questions.explanation: Skin discoloration Clofazimine can cause reddish-black or orange skin discoloration within weeks of therapy and can discolor hair and bodily fluid. This side effect is dose-related and is slowly reversible upon discontinuation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q7

questions.stem: A patient recently started taking medication for active pulmonary tuberculosis. He has been taking his medications regularly, and his pulmonary symptoms have been improving. Unfortunately, he has begun to notice visual changes, including decreased visual acuity and disturbance in his perception of color.
questions.lead_in: Which of his medications is the most likely culprit?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol The most important complication of ethambutol therapy is optic neuritis, which can manifest as decreased visual acuity, restriction of visual fields, and disturbance of color vision. Other important side effects of antituberculous medications include hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, hypersensitivity reactions, bone marrow suppression, and orange discoloration of bodily fluids.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q38

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman had an acid-fast bacilli identified in her sputum culture. She had a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and CKD stage III.
questions.lead_in: What medication can be given without dose adjustment for her renal impairment?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline Doxycycline does not require dose adjustment due to renal impairment. Amikacin, imipenem–cilastatin, ciprofloxacin, and sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim would all require dose adjustments for renal impairment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q5

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of general malaise, anorexia, nausea, and two emetic episodes. She was on her fourth week of treatment with rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for TB uveitis. One week earlier, she had nasal congestion and sore throat that was self-limited, for which she took acetaminophen twice a day. Investigations: Total white cell count 8.3 ×109/L AST 410 U/L ALT 389 U/L Total bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL INR 1.1 Alkaline phosphatase 85 U/L Albumin 42g/L
questions.lead_in: What is unlikely to have caused her drug-induced liver injury?
questions.explanation: Ethambutol Acetaminophen is a common known cause of drug-induced liver injury. The most common antituberculosis drugs to be associated with liver toxicity are INH > PZA > RIF . EMB is not a common cause of hepatotoxicity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q17

questions.question: Indications for pyridoxine supplementation with isoniazid.

parts.text: What are 4 indications for the use of pyridoxine with isoniazid (INH)?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 indications for the use of pyridoxine with INH?

questions.model_answer: INH promotes pyridoxine excretion and predisposes to neuropathy; supplementation (10-50 mg/day) is indicated in: (1) pregnancy (and the immediate postpartum period); (2) poor nutrition/malnutrition; (3) chronic alcoholism; (4) diabetes mellitus or uremia (renal failure). Slow acetylators with high plasma INH levels are also at higher risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: Breastfed infants and symptomatic HIV infection are commonly cited indications (ATS/CDC/IDSA) not explicit in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: High dose INH; Pregnancy; Breast feeding; Meat and milk-deficient diets; Breastfed infants; Nutritional deficiencies; Symptomatic HIV infection.

questions.question: Why do you need to counsel women about the use of alternatives to oral contraceptive pills while on antituberculous therapy?

parts.text: Why do you need to counsel women about the use of alternatives to oral contraceptive pills (OCP) while on antituberculous therapy?

parts_raw.text: Why do you need to counsel women about the use of alternatives to OCP while on antituberculous therapy?

questions.model_answer: Rifampin is a potent inducer of the cytochrome P-450 microsomal enzyme system and increases hepatic metabolism of many drugs, including estrogens/progestins in OCPs, reducing contraceptive levels and efficacy and risking contraceptive failure. Women should use an alternative or additional non-hormonal method (e.g., barrier/condoms). Induction can persist for weeks after rifampin is stopped.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin is an inducer of cytochrome p450 and will increase the metabolism of OCP thereby decreasing its efficacy. Use condoms.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of action for pyrazinamide causing hyperuricemia?

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action for pyrazinamide causing hyperuricemia?

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action for pyrazinamide causing hyperuricemia?

questions.model_answer: Pyrazinoic acid, the active metabolite of pyrazinamide, reduces renal tubular excretion of uric acid (competing with uric acid for renal elimination), producing urate retention. This causes asymptomatic hyperuricemia in ~50% of recipients, with symptomatic gout occurring mainly in patients with preexisting gout.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell states urate retention/hyperuricemia occurs but the competitive pyrazinoic-acid-for-uric-acid tubular secretion mechanism is established pharmacology beyond the chapter text.

cohort_answer.text: Pyrazinoic acid, the active metabolite of PZA, competes with uric acid for elimination via the kidneys, resulting in asymptomatic hyperuricemia and exacerbations of gout in susceptible individuals.

questions.question: What 2 tests do you need to follow up for patients on ethambutol?

parts.text: What 2 tests do you need to follow up for patients on ethambutol?

parts_raw.text: What 2 tests do you need to follow-up for patients on ethambutol?

questions.model_answer: (1) Visual acuity testing; (2) Red-green color perception (discrimination) testing. Both are obtained at baseline and monitored (monthly if treated >2 months or at higher doses) to detect retrobulbar optic neuritis.

cohort_answer.text: Visual acuity, colour discrimination, renal failure (case reports).

questions.model_answer: a) Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol. b) Rash, most→least likely: (1) pyrazinamide; (2) isoniazid; (3) rifampin. c) Hepatitis, most→least likely: (1) pyrazinamide; (2) isoniazid; (3) rifampin. d) Adverse effect → most likely agent: hepatitis → pyrazinamide (INH close second); rash → pyrazinamide; peripheral neuropathy → isoniazid; optic neuritis / red-green colour loss → ethambutol; hyperuricemia/arthralgia → pyrazinamide; orange body secretions and most drug interactions → rifampin. e) Environmental measures for the bronchoscopy suite: (1) negative-pressure room with adequate air exchanges (≥12/hr); (2) HEPA filtration of exhausted/recirculated air; (3) upper-room ultraviolet germicidal irradiation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Environmental/engineering controls for the bronchoscopy suite are from CDC and CTS infection-control guidance, not this chapter.

questions.question: Describe the specific mechanisms of action for the following anti-tubercular medications.
questions.question_raw: Describe the specific mechanisms of actions for the following anti-tubercular medications.
questions.model_answer: a) Isoniazid: inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, blocking mycobacterial cell wall synthesis (bactericidal). b) Rifamycins (rifampin/rifabutin/rifapentine): inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta-subunit, rpoB); human RNA polymerase is insensitive. c) Linezolid: oxazolidinone that inhibits initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit (antimycobacterial toxicity relates to inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis). d) Levofloxacin: inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, the enzyme maintaining DNA supercoiling needed for chromosomal replication. e) Bedaquiline: a diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, becoming bactericidal over several days.

questions.question: A patient with tuberculosis is being treated with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
questions.question_raw: Patient with TB is being tx with INH/RIF/PZA/ETH.

parts.text: Name 3 drugs that will have drug interactions with this combination and why they are interacting.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 drugs that will have drug interactions with this combination and why they are interacting?

questions.model_answer: (1) Warfarin - rifampin induces CYP450, increasing warfarin metabolism and lowering warfarin levels/INR (loss of anticoagulation). (2) Oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol/progestin) - rifampin induces their metabolism, reducing levels and contraceptive efficacy. (3) Phenytoin - isoniazid (especially in slow acetylators) inhibits phenytoin metabolism, potentiating phenytoin toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, mental changes). [Methadone or protease inhibitors, via rifampin induction, are equally acceptable.]

cohort_answer.text: Warfarin/Rifampin – induces warfarin metabolism, decreasing warfarin levels. Methadone/Rifampin – induces methadone metabolism, reduces methadone levels. Oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone)/Rifampin – induces OCP metabolism, reducing levels.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of action of rifampin, isoniazid, linezolid, moxifloxacin, and bedaquiline.
questions.question_raw: Describe the mechanism of: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin, Bedaquiline.
questions.model_answer: a) Rifampin: inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta-subunit, rpoB); human RNA polymerase is insensitive. b) Isoniazid: inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, blocking cell wall synthesis (bactericidal). c) Linezolid: oxazolidinone inhibiting initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit; mycobacterial toxicity reflects inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis. d) Moxifloxacin: inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (and topoisomerase IV), disrupting DNA supercoiling required for chromosomal replication. e) Bedaquiline: diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, becoming bactericidal over several days.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, occurring as a result of drug binding in the polymerase subunit deep within the DNA/RNA channel, facilitating direct blocking of elongating RNA. Isoniazid: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, interfering with cell wall synthesis, producing a bactericidal effect; also disrupts DNA, lipid, carbohydrate, and NAD synthesis/metabolism. Linezolid: Inhibits initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosome (contains 5S rRNA, 23S rRNA, 34 proteins); also suppresses production of bacterial toxins such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin, alpha-hemolysin, and TSST-1. Moxifloxacin: Directly inhibits DNA synthesis; binds to DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV, generating DNA cleavage. Bedaquiline: Inhibits bacterial ATP synthase; ATP production is required for cellular energy production and its loss leads to inhibition of mycobacterial growth within hours

questions.question: Name the antimicrobial agent most commonly associated with each of the following.
questions.question_raw: 2. Name the antimicrobial agent most COMMONLY associated with the following:
questions.model_answer: a) Voriconazole. b) Pyrazinamide (via hyperuricemia from inhibited renal urate excretion). c) Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin). d) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (also NSAIDs, metronidazole, IVIG).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the fluoroquinolone-tendinopathy link is within the Quinolones chapter; photopsia (voriconazole), gout (pyrazinamide) and drug-induced aseptic meningitis (TMP-SMX) rest on general Mandell pharmacology/IDSA knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: Photopsia: Voriconazole. Gout: Pyrazinamide. Tendinopathy: Fluoroquinolones e.g. Ciprofloxacin. Aseptic meningitis: Septra, Flagyl.

questions.question: Give examples of drugs or drug classes that prolong the QT interval, using each class only once.
questions.question_raw: In the following examples, please give examples of drugs or drug classes that prolong QT (You can only use the same class once)
questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) — associated with QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors or other QT-prolonging drugs; (2) Fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, levofloxacin).
b) One antiviral: an HIV protease inhibitor (e.g., saquinavir, usually ritonavir-boosted).
c) One antiparasitic: an antimalarial such as chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine or quinine (pentamidine also acceptable).
d) One antimycobacterial: bedaquiline (clofazimine and delamanid also prolong QT).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the macrolide (and fluoroquinolone interaction) QT risk is in this chapter; the antiviral, antiparasitic, and antimycobacterial examples rest on general pharmacology/product labelling and QT-drug lists (e.g., CredibleMeds).

questions.question: Questions on first-line TB drugs and coadministration of antituberculous therapy with antiretrovirals.

parts.text: 4 first-line TB drugs and their significant side effects
Dose adjustments of antiretrovirals with rifamycin and which is preferred
What is the preferred rifamycin? Dose adjustment?

parts_raw.text: 4 first line TB drugs and their significant side effects
Dose adjustments of ARVs with rifamycin and which preferred
What is the rifamycin preferred? Dose adjustment?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Isoniazid - hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy; (2) Rifampin - hepatitis (bilirubin/ALP) and orange discoloration of secretions; (3) Pyrazinamide - hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia/arthralgia; (4) Ethambutol - retrobulbar optic neuritis (loss of acuity/red-green color vision). b) Rifampin strongly induces CYP450 and should NOT be coadministered with PIs (with/without ritonavir); rifabutin is the preferred rifamycin in HIV patients on PI-based regimens because it is a weaker (~50%) inducer. With PIs, reduce rifabutin (e.g., 150 mg/day or 150 mg every other day/3x weekly), as boosted PIs markedly raise rifabutin levels. c) With rifampin, efavirenz needs no dose change (some experts 800 mg if >60 kg); efavirenz AUC falls ~22% with no change in rifampin. Rifampin is not recommended with PIs (PI exposure falls >75-95%); if rifabutin used with efavirenz, increase rifabutin to 450-600 mg. d) Start ART in all HIV/TB co-infected patients: if CD4 <50 cells/mm3, within 2 weeks of starting TB treatment; if CD4 >=50, within 8-12 weeks (2-4 weeks if severe disease). e) Rifabutin is preferred; standard 300 mg daily, but reduce to 150 mg/day or 150 mg every other day / 300 mg 3x weekly with PIs, and increase to 450-600 mg when given with efavirenz.

cohort_answer.text: First line TB drugs and key side effects: Rifampin - hepatotoxicity; INH - hepatotoxicity; Pyrazinamide; Ethambutol. Rifamycin/ARV dosing: Rifabutin preferred (least CYP3A4 inducer); for PIs reduce rifabutin to 150mg daily; ritonavir/cobicistat increases rifabutin levels; EFV can reduce rifabutin levels so use 450mg daily; otherwise usual dose 300mg daily. Efavirenz and PI: do not co-administer with ATV, ATV/c, ATV/r, DRV/c; caution with DRV/r (monitor closely); LPV/r 500/125 BID with EFV standard doses; TPV needs co-administration with RTV at standard doses. TB co-infection ART timing: if CD4<50, start ART within 2 weeks of starting TB tx; if CD4>50, start ART within 8 weeks; if CNS TB, delay ART start for 8 weeks. Preferred rifamycin: Rifabutin (least CYP3A4 inducer); for PIs reduce to 150mg daily; ritonavir/cobicistat increases rifabutin levels; EFV reduces rifabutin levels so use 450mg daily; otherwise usual dose 300mg daily.

questions.question: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (the same agent cannot be reused): two antibiotics, one antiparasitic, and one anti-tuberculous drug.
questions.question_raw: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (cannot reuse the same agent): 2 antibiotics, 1 antiparasitic, 1 anti-TB

parts.text: One anti-tuberculous drug causing QTc prolongation

questions.model_answer:
a) Two antibiotics: (1) A fluoroquinolone — moxifloxacin (greatest QT effect; ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin less so) — blocks cardiac potassium channels, delays repolarization, and can precipitate torsades de pointes. (2) A macrolide — erythromycin (or azithromycin), also a QT-prolonging agent with which quinolone effects are additive.
b) One antiparasitic: quinine (alternatively chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine or mefloquine).
c) One anti-TB drug: bedaquiline (alternatively clofazimine).
questions.beyond_mandell: The quinolone chapter grounds only the antibiotics (fluoroquinolone and erythromycin/macrolide) for QT prolongation; the antiparasitic (quinine/chloroquine) and anti-TB (bedaquiline/clofazimine) agents are established QT-prolongers from general pharmacology/drug-safety references, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, Azithromycin. Antiparasitic: Quinine, Sodium stibogluconate, Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (also possible but rare ~5%). Anti-TB: Clofazimine, Bedaquiline, Linezolid.

questions.question: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (the same agent cannot be reused): two antibiotics, one antiparasitic, and one anti-tuberculous drug.
questions.question_raw: Identify agents of each class that cause QTc prolongation (cannot reuse the same agent) –
questions.model_answer:
a) Two antibiotics: (1) a macrolide — azithromycin (or erythromycin); (2) a fluoroquinolone — moxifloxacin (greatest effect), levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin. Both delay cardiac repolarization via potassium-channel blockade.
b) One antiparasitic: quinine (alternatively chloroquine or mefloquine).
c) One anti-TB drug: bedaquiline (alternatively clofazimine).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the antibiotics (fluoroquinolone and macrolide/erythromycin) are grounded in this quinolone chapter; the antiparasitic (quinine/chloroquine/mefloquine) and anti-TB (bedaquiline/clofazimine) QT-prolonging agents come from general pharmacology/drug-safety references.

cohort_answer.text: 2 antibiotics: Macrolides (Azithromycin), Fluroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Ciprofloxacin). 1 antiparasitic: Quinine, Chloroquine, Mefloquine. 1 anti-TB: Bedaquiline, Clofazimine.
